Root: P(churn) = sigmoid(-2.009 + usageResponse + intlPlanSwitch + usageHinges + stateUnits + areaCodeUnits + accountLengthUnits + linearBackbone). Purely additive in the logit: the seven children share no hidden nodes and interact only through the output sigmoid. All nonlinearity that matters is inside usageResponse (voicemail-gated usage hinge, convex top-usage hinge, and a service-calls gate that opens from 3-4 calls only below the usage hinge). The intl plan is a flat +3.0 offset; the other children are near-affine corrections and per-state offsets. 27 unconnected inputs (22 states, areaCode415, totalDayCalls, totalNightCalls, totalNightCharge) are zero-effect entries.

Evidence: Train n=4000: AUC 0.926 (refit L2 logistic regression 0.843). Every top-level child replaced by its least-squares linear fit jointly: 0.831. Restoring each child's nonlinearity alone onto that: usageResponse +0.094, intlPlanSwitch +0.0002, usageHinges -0.0008, accountLengthUnits -0.0003, others 0. Only usageResponse is far from linear (R2 0.37); the rest have linear R2 >= 0.95. All state one-hots set to 0: AUC 0.918. KernelSHAP on the root (train, max_samples 300, probability scale), mean |SHAP|: 4344 0.064, 6711 0.061, 10552 0.060, 879 0.057, identity_lin 0.029, 2297 0.016, 24997 0.014, all others < 0.005; unconnected inputs ~2.5e-4 (KernelSHAP noise; their true effect is exactly 0).

ann_89.text: This part acts on 1795 of 4000 training customers (45%).
For a typical customer it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 2% without this part to about 3% with it.
In the training data, 453 of these 1795 customers had churn.

A higher total daytime minutes clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, and even more so if total evening minutes is above 201 minutes (in an uneven way for patients with total evening minutes above 201 minutes): for a typical customer, total daytime minutes going from 112 minutes to 249 minutes moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 1% to about 7% if total evening minutes is above 201 minutes, and from about 1% to about 2% if total evening minutes is at or below 201 minutes.
Other effects: customer-service calls past about 3 calls raises it slowly at first, then faster; total daytime minutes past about 198 minutes raises it in an uneven way.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: a higher total daytime minutes raises it in an uneven way; a higher customer-service calls raises it slowly at first, then faster; total daytime charge past about 40.05 US dollars raises it in an uneven way; Louisiana (rather than any other state) lowers it; a voice-mail plan (rather than no voice-mail plan) lowers it; a higher total evening minutes raises it in an uneven way; a higher total night-time minutes raises it in an uneven way; a higher total daytime charge raises it in an uneven way; and one still smaller effect listed in the evidence table (on the training data only).

ann_90.text: This part acts on 380 of 4000 training customers (10%); nearly all of them are customers with an international plan.
For a typical customer it acts on, it clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 1% without this part to about 24% with it.
In the training data, 161 of these 380 customers had churn.

The model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan than if the customer has no international plan, and even more so if the customer is in Iowa: for a typical customer, going from no international plan to an international plan moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 1% to about 31% if the customer is in Iowa, and from about 1% to about 15% if state is something other than Iowa, Missouri.
